title: Design a URL shortener
prompt: Design a service that turns a long URL into a short link, and redirects anyone who opens the short link to the original URL.

functional: Create a short link for a given long URL.
Opening a short link redirects to the original URL.
The creator may choose a custom alias instead of a generated code.
A link may be given an expiry time, after which it stops redirecting.
non_functional: Redirects keep working when link creation is unavailable.
A link that was created successfully is never lost.
Redirects are fast; the service adds little latency in front of the destination.
Two different long URLs never receive the same short code.
assumptions: A stored link record is about 500 bytes.

key_points.text: One call creates a link: it takes the long URL, an optional alias and an optional expiry, and returns the short code. One call resolves a link: a GET on the short code answers with a redirect.
The server SHOULD send the destination in a Location header field, which the user agent MAY use for automatic redirection.
301 (Moved Permanently) says the resource has a new permanent URI, and a 301 response is heuristically cacheable.

302 (Found) says the resource resides temporarily under a different URI and the client ought to continue to use the original URI for future requests. 302 is not among the heuristically cacheable status codes.

The choice of status code is therefore a choice about load and control. 301 lets clients and caches stop asking the service; 302 keeps every click coming to it, which expiry and click counting depend on.
One record per link, keyed by the short code, holding the long URL, the creation time, the expiry time and the creator.

A store such as DynamoDB feeds the partition key value to a hash function to choose the partition, and AWS recommends a partition key with a large number of distinct values relative to the number of items.
The short code is unique per record, which makes it a partition key of the kind that recommendation describes, and every redirect looks a record up by exactly that key.
Twitter's Snowflake produces a 64-bit ID from 41 bits of millisecond time, 10 bits of machine ID and 12 bits of sequence number, without the generating machines having to coordinate.
A generated numeric ID can be written in base 62 to give the short code. A custom alias is stored under the same key, so creating one must fail if the key already exists.

notes.text: Clients reach a pool of stateless link service instances through a load balancer. The service reads through a cache and falls back to the database, which holds every link.
Facebook's memcache is a demand-filled look-aside cache: the web server asks the cache first, and on a miss reads the database and populates the cache.
Facebook attributes the value of caching to a workload dominated by fetching data. This Question's Scope has the same shape, with 100 redirects per link created.
Dynamo replicates each data item at N hosts, and reports (3, 2, 2) as the common (N, R, W) configuration.

checks.title: The service reads through a cache in front of the database
checks.miss: No Connection from a Service to a Cache carries the read path, or the Service has no Database behind it.

rationale.text: In Facebook's look-aside pattern the web server requests a value from the cache first and only on a miss retrieves it from the database.

checks.title: Every Database keeps more than one copy of the data
checks.miss: There is no Database, or a Database has a replication factor of 1.

rationale.text: Dynamo replicates each data item at N hosts to achieve high availability and durability.

checks.title: Every Database is partitioned on a stated key
checks.miss: There is no Database, or a Database has no partitioning or no partition key.

rationale.text: DynamoDB uses the partition key value as input to a hash function whose output determines the partition in which an item is stored.

checks.title: More than one Service instance sits behind a Load balancer
checks.miss: No Load balancer connects to a Service, or a Service runs as a single instance.

rationale.text: nginx marks a server as failed when a response fails with an error and tries to avoid selecting it for subsequent requests.

checks.title: Every Cache has an eviction policy that frees memory
checks.miss: A Cache has no eviction policy, or uses noeviction.

rationale.text: Under noeviction Redis returns an error for commands that would cache new data once the memory limit is reached; allkeys-lru is described as a good default.

deep_dives.prompt: How do you generate short codes that never collide, without every creation going through one coordinator?

key_points.text: Twitter required that machines generating IDs should not have to coordinate with each other, for high availability within and across data centres.
A Snowflake ID is 41 bits of millisecond time, 10 bits of configured machine ID (up to 1024 machines) and 12 bits of sequence number (4096 per machine before rolling over).
Snowflake depends on the system clock: it should be kept accurate with NTP, and the generator protects against clocks that run backwards.

Uniqueness then comes from each service instance holding a distinct machine ID, and the code is the ID written in base 62. A full 64-bit ID is longer than the 7 characters the estimate calls for, so shorter codes need fewer bits or a different generator.

deep_dives.prompt: One link goes viral. What stops the redirect traffic from reaching the database?

key_points.text: With a look-aside cache only a miss reaches the database; the result is then put in the cache for later reads.
Redis's documentation recommends allkeys-lru when a subset of elements is accessed far more often than the rest.
A thundering herd arises when a key has heavy read and write activity and writes keep invalidating the cached value; Facebook's leases address it.
A 301 response is heuristically cacheable, so clients and intermediaries may reuse it without asking the service again.
A link is written once and then only read, so the write-driven invalidation behind a thundering herd is rare here; the first miss after an eviction is the case to think about.

deep_dives.prompt: How is 3 TB of links spread across machines, and what happens when one machine fails?

key_points.text: In consistent hashing a key is hashed to a position on a ring and assigned to the first node clockwise from it, and the arrival or departure of a node only affects its immediate neighbours.
Dynamo assigns each node multiple points on the ring, virtual nodes, to even out data and load.
Each item is replicated at N hosts: the coordinator stores it and replicates it at the N-1 clockwise successors.
With R + W > N the system behaves like a quorum system, and latency is dictated by the slowest of the R or W replicas.
